 1          23andMe’s motion for an extension pleads in the tone of reasonable order. The case

 2   should be stayed, in 23andMe’s view, until a case management conference, which shouldn’t

 3   happen until its motion to stay based on the pending JPML decision is decided, and in turn, the

 4   JPML decides whether to form an MDL. What the motion doesn’t do is explain the story that is

 5   going on behind the scenes. In short, 23andMe is seeking to suspend the litigation while

 6   launching a plan to sell off its users’ data to any pharmaceutical research company willing to

 7   bite. See Thomas Germain, 23andMe Admits ‘Mining’ Your DNA Data Is Its Last Hope,

 8   GIZMODO (Feb. 13, 2024), https://gizmodo.com/23andme-admits-mining-your-dna-data-is-its-

 9   last-hope-1851252582.
10          Plaintiffs in this case (the “Melvin Plaintiffs”) have raised urgent questions with
11   23andMe about its apparent attempt to solve its public financial woes with a fire sale of user
12   data that violates numerous laws—and exposes the Class to even greater privacy harms than
13   what they have already suffered. While the Melvin Plaintiffs are entirely in favor of good order
14   (and have made suggestions about how to accomplish that to 23andMe) the company is
15   leveraging the procedural complexity of the sheer number of cases on file to give it a window
16   to execute plans that harm the Class. For the reasons below, Plaintiffs must oppose.
17          A. 23andMe Announces Its Plan to Widely Sell Its Users’ Data for Data Mining
18          Earlier this week, in an interview with Wired, 23andMe’s CEO Anne Wojcicki

19   admitted that 23andMe is intending to—in her own words—offer its users’ genetic information

20   up to “different organizations” to “mine” the data for drug discovery. Emily Mullin, 23andMe

21   Is Under Fire. Its Founder Remains ‘Optimistic’, WIRED (Feb. 12, 2024),

22   https://bit.ly/3OHbGqr. CEO Wojcicki credits 23andMe with assembling the kind of “really

23   monster-size, really significantly large data sets” that allow pharmaceutical companies to

24   profitably mine data. See id. This public offer was widely reported on Tuesday, including by

25   Gizmodo, with the key context that this plan comes as the company is looking to plug the

26   financial holes that are tanking its stock. Germain, supra.

27          23andMe’s plan to sell off data to unidentified pharmaceutical partners is flatly contrary

28   to 23andMe’s promises to its users. Will The Information I Provide Be Shared With Third

Re:    Melvin, et al. v. 23andMe, Inc., Case No. 3:24-cv-00487 (N.D. Cal.)

Counsel:

         We write in response to 23andMe’s announcement that it intends to sell customers’
genetic data to third-party organizations. See Thomas Germain, 23andMe Admits ‘Mining’ Your
DNA Data Is Its Last Hope, GIZMODO (Feb. 13, 2024), https://gizmodo.com/23andme-admits-
mining-your-dna-data-is-its-last-hope-1851252582. This is a drastic, and seemingly urgent,
expansion on what was previously a one-off agreement with GlaxoSmithKline. Paired with the
fact that the company is telling anyone who will listen that it is on the verge of bankruptcy, we
are—we hope unsurprisingly—incredibly concerned about the fate of the genetic information
that is in the company’s hands, as well as where the company’s focus is at this time. When the
company is publicly aimed at squeezing every last drop of profit out of its customers’ genetic
information, we have fair questions about what steps the company has taken and will take to
protect the extraordinarily sensitive data that customers have provided to it.

        In short, we’d like to further understand what it is the company is planning to do and, in
light of the company’s insinuations about its own limited resources, whether it has actually
expended the necessary resources to protect customer data rather than sell it.

        To be clear, if the plan is as described by CEO Wojcicki, we view it as facially violative
of the law for every class member, and particularly those vulnerable class members who have
already been targeted—including specifically for “research”—on the Dark Web. 23andMe
represents to its customers that their genetic information will not be sold without their express
consent, yet it now seeks to sell access to their data on a scale seemingly limited only by the
number of willing buyers. See Will The Information I Provide Be Shared With Third Parties?,

23ANDME.COM (“23andMe does not sell, lease, or rent your Genetic Information or sensitive
Personal Information without receiving your explicit consent.”).

         Moreover, selling access to customers’ genetic information without specific and separate
consent for each disclosure constitutes unlawful conduct under the California Unfair
Competition Law, Cal. Bus. & Prof Code § 17200 et seq. (“UCL”). The California Genetic
Privacy Act requires “separate and express consent” for “[e]ach transfer or disclosure of the
consumer’s genetic data or biological sample to a third party other than to a service provider,
including the name of the third party to which the consumer’s genetic data or biological sample
will be transferred or disclosed.” Cal. Civ. Code § 56.181(a)(2)(D). 23andMe’s Research
Consent Document, 23ANDME.COM, https://www.23andme.com/about/consent/ (“Research
Consent Document”), indicates that it shares customers’ genetic information with “non-profit
organizations, pharmaceutical companies, [and] academic institutions,” and specifically notes
that it “will not ask [customers] for separate permission every time [it] share[s]” customers’
genetic information. This vague, blanket consent practice does not comply with the California
law and, consequently, violates the UCL.

        This practice also violates the Illinois Genetic Information Privacy Act (“GIPA”) and
other state genetic privacy statutes. As relevant here, GIPA only permits disclosure to a “person
designated in a specific written legally effective authorization.” 410 ILCS 513/30 (emphasis
added); see also Or. Rev. Stat. Ann. § 192.539 (permitting disclosure only when it “is
specifically authorized by the tested individual . . . by signing a consent form prescribed by rules
of the Oregon Health Authority”). 23andMe’s generic Research Consent Document and its
Individual Data Sharing Consent form—neither of which name the entities with which 23andMe
shares customers’ genetic information—do not come close to meeting these standards.

           B. Identify any new information security protection software or hardware you have
              implemented since the breach, including but not limited to, encryption,
              antivirus/antimalware/endpoint detection and response software, network or web
              application firewalls, intrusion detection or prevention systems, data loss
              prevention, access control, or others.
           C. Identify and describe any other threat detection or mitigation tools that you have
              put in place, including but not limited to:
                  1. Has 23andMe implemented CAPTCHA for all log-in attempts?

 1       I.       INTRODUCTION

 2             This Court should extend 23andMe’s deadline to respond to the complaint to thirty (30) days after

 3   the CMC because extending the deadline will promote judicial efficiency, avoid the risk of potentially

 4   inconsistent rulings, and help coordinate the dozens of related cases currently pending before this Court.1

 5   As of filing, Plaintiffs’ counsel—who is the only plaintiffs’ firm to not participate in the January 31, 2024

 6   mediation—has not advised whether they will oppose this motion for more time, despite 23andMe’s

 7   repeated requests for Plaintiffs’ position.

 8             Since the Related Cases were filed, 23andMe has operated on two parallel tracks to ensure the

 9   efficient administration of this litigation. 23andMe has worked to streamline the pending litigation to a

10   single timeline by filing a Motion to Transfer Actions to the Northern District of California Pursuant to 18

11   U.S.C. § 1407 for Coordinated or Consolidated Pretrial Proceedings with the Judicial Panel on Multidistrict

12   Litigation, MDL No. 3098 (the “MDL Motion”), filing a Motion to Stay the Related Cases until the JPML

13   makes a determination on the MDL Motion (the “Motion to Stay”), and, where necessary, stipulating to

14   continue deadlines. At the same time, 23andMe has worked with plaintiffs to resolve the claims arising

15   from the Incident by, among other things, engaging in a mediation on January 31, 2024.

16             This Court should grant 23andMe’s motion for a brief extension for three reasons:

17             First, the parties’ and judicial resources will be conserved in favor of judicial economy if the cases

18   are on a single timeline, which extending 23andMe’s deadline to respond to Plaintiffs’ complaint would

19   allow.

20             Second, if 23andMe’s deadline to respond to the complaint is not continued, then 23andMe and the

21   putative classes will be prejudiced by potentially inconsistent proceedings here and in the thirty-one (31)

22   other Related Cases.

23             Third, a brief continuance will not prejudice plaintiffs. Indeed, most plaintiffs’ counsel in the

24   Related Cases have already agreed to the requested continuance. Guyon Decl., ¶ 4.

25       II.      PROCEDURAL AND FACTUAL BACKGROUND

26             In early October 2023, 23andMe learned that certain customer profile information, which users had

 1   elected to share with up to thousands of other DNA relatives through the DNA Relatives feature, was

 2   accessed from individual 23andMe.com user accounts without authorization. Upon learning of the

 3   unauthorized access, 23andMe promptly began investigating the matter and notified customers and law

 4   enforcement of the Incident. After 23andMe discovered and promptly disclosed the Incident, forty (40)

 5   putative class action lawsuits in which plaintiffs assert claims arising from the Incident have been filed in

 6   state and federal courts around the country, primarily in the Northern District of California.2

 7             On December 21, 2023, 23andMe filed a Motion to Transfer Actions to the Northern District of

 8   California Pursuant to 18 U.S.C. § 1407 for Coordinated or Consolidated Pretrial Proceedings with the

 9   Judicial Panel on Multidistrict Litigation, MDL No. 3098 (the “MDL Motion”). Santana at ECF No. 34.

10             On December 29, 2023, Defendants requested this Court enter a stay of all proceedings until the

11   JPML rules on Defendant’s MDL Motion (the “Motion to Stay”) and filed a Re-Notice of the Motion to

12   Stay to correct the briefing schedule on January 5, 2024. The Motion to Stay is set for hearing on February

13   22, 2024. See Santana at ECF Nos. 37, 44.

14             On January 17, 2024, the Court vacated the CMC set for January 23, 2024 in the Related Cases and

15   ordered the CMC be reset to 30 days after the Court rules on Defendant's filed Motion to Stay.

16             Plaintiffs filed the Complaint here on January 26, 2024, and filed a Motion to Appoint Interim

17   Leadership on the same day. In the Motion to Appoint Interim Leadership, Plaintiffs made clear they would

18   not participate in the mediation scheduled for January 31, 2024 and criticized the mediation and its

19   participants. ECF No. 4. The Court denied the Motion to Appoint Interim Leadership on February 2, 2024.

20   ECF No. 15.

21             Plaintiffs served the Summons and Complaint on Defendants on January 29, 2024. Defendant’s

22   deadline to respond is, therefore, February 19, 2024, before the Court rules on 23andMe’s Motion to Stay

23   filed before this case. ECF No. 9; Santana at ECF Nos. 37, 44.

24             23andMe requested that Plaintiffs stipulate to extend 23andMe’s response date to align with the

25   Related Cases on February 1, 2024. Guyon Decl. ¶ 6. To date, Plaintiffs’ counsel has not advised whether

26   they will grant 23andMe its requested stipulation or oppose this motion for a continuance. Id. However,

27   counsel in thirty (30) of the Related Cases have agreed either to stay their cases pending the MDL Motion

 1   or continue 23andMe’s deadline to respond until thirty (30) days after the CMC in the Related Cases.

 2   Guyon Decl. ¶ 4; see also Lamons v. 23andMe, Inc., 3:23-cv-05178 at ECF No. 19 (N.D. Cal. Oct. 9, 2023);

 3   Berman et al v. 23andMe, Inc., 3:23-cv-05345 (N.D. Cal. Oct. 19, 2023) at ECF No. 16; Tulchinsky v.

 4   23andMe, Inc., 3:23-cv-05369 (N.D. Cal. Oct. 19, 2023) at ECF No. 15.

 5      III.      ARGUMENT

 6             Good cause supports the brief continuance requested by this Motion. Under Fed. R. Civ. P.

 7   6(b)(1)(A), the Court may, for good cause, extend the time by which a party must act within a specified

 8   time. “Good cause” is a non-rigorous standard and is broadly construed. Ahanchian v. Xenon Pictures, Inc.,

 9   624 F.3d 1253, 1259 (9th Cir. 2010). “Consequently, requests for extensions of time made before the

10   applicable deadline has passed should normally . . . be granted in the absence of bad faith on the part of the

11   party seeking relief or prejudice to the adverse party.” Id. (internal quotations and citations omitted).

12             1) The Proposed Continuance Will Conserve The Parties’ And Court’s Resources

13             Extending 23andMe’s deadline to respond to the complaint would allow the parties to brief the

14   allegations, claims, and issues once a consolidated amended complaint is filed for the Related Cases or for

15   all the federal courts where actions are pending nationwide. Otherwise, the parties will undoubtedly be

16   forced to relitigate and re-brief the arguments made here before all the other Related Cases. See Nichols v.

17   DePuy Orthopaedics, Inc., 2011 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 135881, at *8 (N.D. Cal. Nov. 2, 2011) (recognizing

18   denying motion would “potentially impose a significant burden on Defendant, insofar as it would be forced

19   to engage in duplicative litigation”). Allowing this matter to proceed before the others would create a

20   “substantial risk of hardship and inequity” to 23andMe and be “a needless use of time and resources.”

21   A.H.M. v. Uber Techs., Inc., No. 23-CV-03482-JSC, 2023 WL 6199179, at *2 (N.D. Cal. Sept. 22, 2023).

22             2) The Continuance Will Avoid Potentially Inconsistent Rulings

23             Denying the proposed continuance would not only cause “unnecessary proceedings” but also risk

24   “inconsistent rulings on recurring questions of law and fact.” Acosta-Smith v. Equifax Inc., 2018 WL

25   1155981, at *4 (C.D. Cal. Mar. 5, 2018) (staying data breach litigation pending JPML transfer). Indeed,

26   Plaintiffs bring the same allegations and claims here as many of the Related Cases—e.g., claims for

27   negligence, under California Unfair Competition Law (UCL), and for injunctive relief. And all the cases

28   arise out of the same Incident. Further, in this matter, Plaintiffs seek to represent the same putative class of

 1   United States residents allegedly affected by the Incident as plaintiffs do in most of the Related Cases.

 2   Accordingly, absent a continuance, inconsistent ruling for the same putative classes for the same claims is

 3   likely unavoidable.

 4             3) A Short Delay Will Not Prejudice Plaintiffs

 5             The brief stay will not prejudice plaintiffs. Any delay from the proposed continuance “is relatively

 6   short and therefore potential prejudice is minimal.” Acosta-Smith, 2018 WL 1155981, at *4. Plaintiffs’

 7   counsel in almost all other Related Cases have already agreed to the requested continuance, which further

 8   demonstrates the lack of prejudice. Guyon Decl., ¶ 4. If anything, the continuance will benefit plaintiffs. It

 9   will allow plaintiffs to coordinate in drafting a consolidated amended complaint and briefing the common

10   claims at issue in all of these cases.

11             Importantly, any potential prejudice to plaintiffs was mitigated because 23andMe brought this

12   motion quickly without delay. In fact, the same day this Court issued an Order relating this case to Santana

13   (ECF No. 14), counsel for 23andMe reached out to Plaintiffs’ counsel to request if Plaintiffs would continue

14   23andMe’s deadline to respond to the complaint until 30 days after the CMC. Guyon Decl., ¶ 6. As such,

15   there is no prejudice to plaintiffs as a result of the minor extension 23andMe requests.

16       IV.      CONCLUSION

17             For the foregoing reasons, 23andMe respectfully requests that this Court continue 23andMe’s

18   deadline to respond to Plaintiffs’ complaint until thirty (30) days after the CMC.
